cim_eredeti: Multiplayer Nodes: Build Krea Workflows Together, Live
szoveg_eredeti:
By the Krea Team. Published October 22, 2026.

Krea Nodes is now multiplayer. You and your team can open the same Nodes project and edit it together. Everyone sees the same canvas, and changes show up as they happen.

Until now, sharing a workflow meant sending a link, waiting for feedback, then making the changes yourself. With Multiplayer Nodes, the art director can rewire the prompt while the designer swaps the reference image and the producer queues the video step. All of it happens on one canvas, and nobody has to email final_v7_REAL.json around.

Live cursors, shared runs, and sharing that fits how your team works.

Multiplayer Nodes is real-time collaboration for Krea’s node-based workflow editor. A Nodes project is a graph: image, video, and text nodes connected by edges, where each node’s output feeds the next one. Multiplayer means several people can build and run that graph at the same time:

Say your team is making a campaign for a glossy red ceramic mushroom lamp. One person drops the product shot and a color moodboard onto the canvas. Another wires them into a few image nodes, one per scene: a bedroom at blue hour, a desert at golden hour, a swimming pool.

Product shot + moodboard → scene variations, built and run together in Nodes

While the art director tweaks the desert prompt, the designer can see their cursor parked on that node. They leave it alone and refine the pool scene instead. When someone hits run, the whole team watches the results come in. Nobody screen-shares, and nobody asks “can you send me the latest version?”

Open any Nodes project and click Share. The dialog gives you three levels of general access, plus individual invites:

To invite someone directly, type their name in Add people from your workspace…, pick them, and choose Can view or Can edit. Edit access applies only within the project’s own workspace.

If a person has their own grant and also gets access through a workspace share, the higher level applies. For example, a teammate invited as a viewer can still edit if the whole workspace has edit access.

Viewers see the structure of the workflow: the nodes, how they connect, and the inputs. They don’t see generated outputs or run history, and they can’t run anything. They can duplicate the project to make their own copy and remix it, which makes a public link a handy way to share a reusable workflow template.

Anyone with edit access can run nodes. Each run is visible to everyone in the project, and finished outputs are saved to the node’s history for all editors.

Whoever starts a run pays for it. Jobs are billed to the person who submits them, in their active workspace. When you start a chain, your tab submits each next step, and the chain keeps running if you switch to another tab. Other collaborators just watch the results arrive.

Krea’s Agent and MCP clients edit Nodes projects through the same operations as people do. When you ask the Agent to add a step or rewire a graph, its changes sync to everyone on the canvas, like a teammate’s would.
